On the night of Ramchandra Ray's escape, Udayaditya holds all the power over Sitaram: he demands the door be opened, draws his sword when Sitaram hesitates, and—since Sitaram refuses to raise arms against the prince who saved his life twice—Udayaditya takes Sitaram's weapon and binds him "from head to foot" with his own cloth at Sitaram's own request, leaving him lying there as Udayaditya walks free. On the night of Udayaditya's escape from prison, this dynamic is completely inverted: it is now Sitaram who holds the power and takes the initiative, coming to the dark cell during the fire alarm, throwing open the door, grabbing Udayaditya and almost carrying him out. Udayaditya, long confined and disoriented, is reduced to helplessness—asking Sitaram "What should I do? Where should I go?"—and can only follow as Sitaram leads him away. Thus the relationship shifts from Udayaditya overpowering and binding a submissive Sitaram to facilitate his own escape, to Sitaram actively rescuing a passive, dependent Udayaditya.

Pratapaditya's initial plan was to have two Pathan men ambush and kill Basanta Ray on the road to Jessore when he stopped at the inn in Simultali. This plan failed because one of the Pathans, Khan Saheb, could not bring himself to commit the murder—he lured Basanta Ray's retainers away with a false story of a dacoit attack, then confessed the plot to Basanta Ray and Udayaditya and sought the old king's protection instead of killing him.

The assassination finally succeeds when Pratapaditya sends Muktiyar Khan with a signed written order sentencing Basanta Ray to death. After reading the order in his own palace at Raigarh, Basanta Ray calmly accepts his fate, finishes his evening prayers, prostrates himself before his deity chanting on his prayer beads, and says "Saheb, now!"—at which point Muktiyar Khan summons Abdul, who enters with a drawn sword and beheads him, leaving a stream of blood flowing in the room.

1) In the **inner quarters (women's apartments) of the Jessore palace**, disguised as a **middle-aged woman** — there Rammohan recognized him, lifted him into the air, swung him around threatening to kill him, seized him by the throat, then bound him with a shawl and carried him out over his shoulder like a sack.

2) In the **king's chamber (the room where the king sat, at Chandradwip)**, appearing as the **court jester** (in his own identity, without disguise) — after his mocking remark about Vibha, Rammohan rushed forward, grabbed him by the scruff of the neck, and threw him out of the room.

The Rajmahishi secretly had Matangini fetch what was presented as medicine from the widow Mangala (actually Rukmini), who spent five days preparing it as a poison—complete with mantras and rituals so that Udayaditya would feel no pity when Surma died—and this poison, administered to Surma on the eve of her departure, killed her.

Vibha's refusal leads to the king, Ramchandra Ray, feeling insulted and, to avenge that humiliation, deciding to take another wife. As a result, when Vibha finally travels to Chandradwip, she arrives on the very day of the king's wedding — she learns that there is no place for her in her husband's palace, and all her hopes of happiness are shattered like a mirage.

Rukmini obtains the ring through emotional manipulation: during a stormy night she visits Udayaditya, tearfully claims he ruined her, and asks for his love; when she tries to sit on Surma's bed and he desperately begs her not to, she demands "that ring on your finger" instead. Udayaditya pulls it off and throws it down, and Rukmini takes it away. Because the ring bears a seal engraved with the Yubaraj's (Udayaditya's) name, Sitaram and Bhagavat are able to use it to stamp a forged petition—written as if Udayaditya himself were complaining of treason against Pratapaditya to the Emperor in order to seize the kingdom for himself. Bhagavat then carries this sealed petition to Pratapaditya, claiming he intercepted it from a fleeing servant of Udayaditya who was taking it toward Delhi. The authentic royal seal on the forged document convinces Pratapaditya of its genuineness, and despite his minister's objections that such an act is unbelievable, he orders Udayaditya imprisoned.

Ramchandra Ray's midnight escape set off a chain reaction: because the guards Sitaram and Bhagavat failed to stop Udayaditya from forcing open the inner quarters that night, they were dismissed from their jobs and left destitute. Out of compassion for them, Udayaditya fixed a monthly stipend for both men. When Pratapaditya learned of this, he was enraged and explicitly forbade any further financial help to them. Defying this order, Surma took the burden upon herself and secretly arranged to send the stipends through her trusted maid—but the maid confided in Mangala, and word of the secret payments reached Pratapaditya. In retaliation, he issued the decree ordering Surma to be sent to her paternal home, ultimately threatening to imprison Udayaditya unless she complied—forcing Surma to accept exile.

The song expresses the anguish of utter desolation—the grief of a man whose loved ones have vanished, leaving him with nothing but emptiness: "What was there has gone away," those who were once his "no longer answer my call," and he questions how he can go on living with only himself. It captures both nostalgic longing and bereavement.

Basanta Ray sings it in two contrasting contexts:

1. **Alone at Raigarh:** Sitting on his palace veranda at sunset, without his sitar (whose strings have broken), he hums the song quietly to himself. Here it arises spontaneously from wistful yearning—he remembers the joy he once felt traveling to Jessore to see his loved ones, and wonders whether he will ever see them again. It is a private, melancholy meditation on absence and lost joy.

2. **At Jessore, with Vibha:** After learning of Udayaditya's imprisonment, he travels to Jessore and finds the royal household dark and deserted—Surma's room silent and empty, Vibha standing alone like "the sole broken remnant of a happy family." There, taking Vibha's hand, he slowly sings "I alone am left behind!" aloud. In this second context, the song is no longer private longing but a shared, heart-rending lament over a loss that has actually come to pass—the family that once filled the house with joy and song is truly gone.

Rukmini's failure to stop the escape set off the chain of events that ended in Basanta Ray's execution:

1. **She fails at the canal:** When she reaches the boat, she can only attack Sitaram, scream her curse, and jump into the water—the boat departs with Udayaditya and Basanta Ray, and the escape succeeds.

2. **She exposes the conspiracy:** Enraged that "nothing came of it," she goes to Pratapaditya's court and reveals that the Yubaraj escaped the previous night with the old king of Raigarh, and that Sitaram set the fires as part of the plot among the three of them.

3. **She confirms Udayaditya's location:** Pratapaditya sends men with her; they verify that Udayaditya is in Raigarh. This prompts Pratapaditya to dispatch the Pathan commander Muktiyar Khan with a secret order.

4. **She enables Udayaditya's capture:** At Raigarh, it is Rukmini who spots Udayaditya in the field and cries out, "Here! Here is your Yubaraj—right here!"—allowing Muktiyar Khan's soldiers to seize him.

5. **Her success dooms Basanta Ray:** Once Udayaditya is captured, Muktiyar Khan proceeds to carry out Pratapaditya's second, signed order—the death sentence for the King of Raigarh. Despite Udayaditya's frantic pleas that the order was meant only for if he could not be found, Muktiyar insists the clear order must be obeyed, and Basanta Ray is beheaded by Abdul while at prayer.

Thus, because Rukmini could not prevent the escape herself, she instead betrayed the fugitives to Pratapaditya, tracked Udayaditya down, and delivered him into captivity—directly triggering the execution of Basanta Ray.

In Chapter 8, Pratapaditya receives Ramchandra Ray with cold, understated indifference rather than open hostility: the welcome arrangements are minimal (the Dewan arrives late with only 250 men and a small elephant), and when they meet, Pratapaditya shows "not the slightest joy or haste," calmly greets him, turns to ministerial business, interrupts him, and dismisses him with "Go now, my boy, to the inner quarters." This quiet condescension wounds Ramchandra's pride so deeply that he leaves realizing "in what way Pratapaditya was superior to him."

In Chapter 19, Ramchandra retaliates in his own court by allowing—and visibly enjoying—daily ridicule of Pratapaditya. His courtiers attack Pratapaditya's lineage and legitimacy, claiming his father had to beg Ramchandra's grandfather for royal anointment and likening his ancestry to an earthworm and a leech; the king smiles, smokes his hookah, and feels "immense pleasure" as these verbal assaults continue daily. He further asserts superiority over Pratapaditya by treating the marriage connection as a stain on his honor—refusing to bring Vibha home on the grounds that bringing "Pratapaditya's daughter into my house" would compromise his dignity.

Thus, while Pratapaditya asserted his superiority through calm, dignified slight, Ramchandra responds with petty, vindictive degradation of Pratapaditya's status in his own court—mocking his ancestry, encouraging flatterers' attacks, and distancing himself from the marital tie—all revealing Ramchandra as small-minded and unable to match Pratapaditya's composed authority.

The older widow, Rukmini, re-enters Udayaditya's life by leaving Raigarh and settling on the outskirts of Jessore under a new name, Mangala. From there she works her way into the palace by befriending its servants and tracking every piece of palace news, while hoping to rule over Udayaditya's heart when he becomes king. She performs tantric rituals and prayers for the deaths of Pratapaditya and Surma, and when these fail, she seizes an opportunity: the Rajmahishi, hearing that a widow named Mangala knows tantra, mantra, and medicine, sends Matangini to secretly fetch medicine from her. Mangala spends five days preparing not medicine but poison, chanting mantras and performing rituals so that the Yubaraj would feel no pity when Surma died. The poison reaches Surma, who dies from it on the eve of her departure from the palace. Later, Rukmini also confronts Udayaditya in person—appearing at night in his darkened chamber, feigning that he had ruined her and left her destitute—to manipulate him, and extracts his ring from him.

Udayaditya's early lament—wishing he had been born "a subject of the lowliest" rather than the sole heir to Pratapaditya's throne, complaining that in a king's family everyone is born an heir and not a son, and recalling how his failure at Hosenkhali made his father give up on him—foreshadows his desire to escape royal life entirely; he even tells Surma he sometimes thinks of leaving everything and going away with her. This wish finally comes true in Chapter 34: after returning to Jessore as a prisoner and concluding in anguish that he is a weak coward whose clinging has destroyed those dearest to him ("No more, I am taking my leave of this world"), he is brought before Pratapaditya. When his father declares him unworthy of the kingdom, Udayaditya agrees and formally pleads, "grant me release from your throne." To prove his sincerity, he takes a solemn oath at the temple before Ma-Kali, witnessed by Pratapaditya, swearing that as long as he lives he will not accept even an iota of the Maharaja's kingdom, will not sit on the throne of Jessore, and will not even touch its royal scepter—invoking the sin of his grand-uncle's murder upon himself if he ever breaks it. Renouncing kingdom and family, he departs for Kashi as an ascetic, asking only for money to establish a guest house and temple in his grand-uncle's name—thus transforming his youthful lament into a binding, formal renunciation.

Ramchandra Ray's letter—declaring that he had renounced Vibha and that she should not be sent to Chandradwip again—was entrusted to the old Nayanchand after Rammohan refused to carry it. Fearing what Pratapaditya might do if the letter reached him, Nayanchand never delivered it to the Maharaj; instead, he secretly handed it over to the Mahishi. The Mahishi, terrified of the consequences, hid the letter's existence from Pratapaditya—she only approached him weeping and spoke of the matter purely hypothetically, asking what would happen "if one day" the son-in-law were to write such a letter, which Pratapaditya dismissed as needless worry. She then showed the letter to Basanta Ray, who advised keeping it secret and sending Vibha at once, reasoning that Ramchandra had written only out of anger that would subside once Vibha returned. Following his counsel, the Mahishi misrepresented the letter to Vibha and announced throughout the household that Ramchandra Ray had written a letter *requesting* that Vibha be sent to her in-laws' house—converting a letter of renunciation into an apparent summons. Deceived by this, Vibha was overjoyed, believing her husband had understood her heart and forgiven her.

Pratapaditya anticipated an escape by water and ordered the canal adjoining the palace—where Ramchandra Ray's boat lay—to be blocked with large Sal wood logs. The blockade did stop the boat after it had gone a short distance, but the trap failed because:

1. **The guards could not reach or harm the boat**: From afar they threw stones, but none reached the boat. They had only swords and no guns; when one guard finally found a flintlock gun, there was no gunpowder or ammunition available.

2. **The boat was carried over the barrier**: While the guards scrambled uselessly for weapons, Rammohan and his followers simply pulled the boat up and over the Sal wood logs, clearing the obstruction.

3. **The pursuit was fatally delayed**: By the time the guards arranged a chase boat, the man sent to fetch it had stopped at Harimudi's shop to smoke tobacco and wake Ramashankar to press him for debt payment. The boat arrived long after it was needed, and the pursuers realized there was no longer any chance of catching Ramchandra's boat, which escaped to the Bhairav river.

Basanta Ray's sitar serves as a barometer of his inner life, and its abandonment mirrors his despair over losing Udayaditya. Once his "eternal companion," the sitar embodied the joy he shared with his loved ones—yet at his departure, his playing falters as tears blur his eyes and choke his throat, forcing him to put it down. He leaves it behind with Udayaditya, declaring he will never play it again, as if music itself has become meaningless without the boy. Later, alone in Raigarh, the sitar is absent from his side while he hums songs of emptiness—"I alone am left behind." When Khan Saheb asks about it, Basanta Ray reveals that although the instrument still exists, "its strings have broken, and it can no longer be tuned"—a metaphor for his own heart. With Udayaditya taken from him and then imprisoned, the source of his music and joy is severed; like the untunable sitar, he remains present in body but incapable of song, expressing only desolation.

Earlier, Udayaditya was known for boldly intervening on behalf of oppressed subjects—Pratapaditya himself complained that Udayaditya "was not like this before," that he went out whenever he pleased, involved himself in the affairs of subjects, and acted against the king's wishes. Before, he would have stopped a royal official who was beating a subject without considering the consequences, and would have tried to protect the victim.

After Surma's death, however, this willingness completely disappeared. A strange, blind fear of Pratapaditya took hold of his mind—his former courage was gone, and he could no longer treat danger as a trifle or fight oppression with all his might. When he learned of an order to have club-wielding men loot and burn the zamindar of Chhapra's estate office, he had his horse readied but then absentmindedly told the servant to take it away, abandoning the mission. When he heard a subject tied to a tree crying for mercy as an official beat him, he could not bear the sight and instead ran inside his house. Likewise, when the stipends of Bhagavat and Sitaram were stopped, he repeatedly resolved to send them money but always hesitated, and the money was never sent. Thus, he changed from a fearless protector of the oppressed into someone paralyzed by hesitation and doubt in every matter—not out of fear for his own life, but because Pratapaditya had become, in his mind, a mysterious entity controlling his every fate.

Sitaram had helped Bhagavat forge a petition—stamped with the Yubaraj's seal—accusing Udayaditya of plotting treason against Pratapaditya, which led to Udayaditya's imprisonment. To undo this, Sitaram set fire to the row of guard huts near the prison, causing all the guards to abandon their posts to fight the blaze. In the resulting chaos, he opened Udayaditya's cell, told him the prison was on fire, and carried him out to freedom in an open field, then led him away to safety.

On the first occasion (Chapter 11), Rammohan rescues Ramchandra Ray from Pratapaditya's palace by rope descent: he twists several very thick, large bed sheets into a huge makeshift rope, ties it to a small pillar on the palace roof overlooking the canal, straps the Maharaj onto his back, climbs hand-over-hand down the rope, grips it with his teeth at the end, and carefully lowers Ramchandra with both hands into the sixty-four-oared boat waiting about seventy cubits below before jumping down himself; they then row off, hauling the boat over sal-wood logs blocking the canal while guards hurl stones.

On the second occasion (Chapter 37), after Vibha faints upon being disowned by the king in the hostile palace, Rammohan simply lifts her unconscious body in his arms, carries her out past the gate, and places her into one of the palanquins standing nearby, taking her away by boat.

In Jessore, Vibha is lavishly adorned by the Mahishi for Ramchandra Ray's arrival—wearing eight thick gold bangles and a huge diamond bracelet on each arm instead of her preferred thin turquoise ones, a large nose ring, and an elaborate hairstyle imposed by the Mahishi, presenting herself as a bejeweled royal bride radiant with joy. By contrast, when she goes to seek him out in Chandradwip after learning of his remarriage, she strips away all royal pretense: she refuses a palanquin ("Am I a queen...? I will go like a common subject, like a beggar-woman"), steps off the boat dressed as an ordinary common woman, walks through the crowd unnoticed, enters the palace unrecognized like any other maidservant—with no welcome—and is mistaken by the king himself for a beggar woman come seeking alms.

For Udayaditya, the window shifts from being a monument to loss into a promise of freedom.

**In the bedchamber after Surma's death**, the window is bound up with grief and denial. It marks the spot where Surma used to sit, which he deliberately leaves empty. Sitting there amid the same moonlight, the same garden, and the same breeze, he clings to the illusion that she cannot truly be gone—on such an evening, how could Surma stay away? Each evening he returns with "a flicker of hope" that opening the door will reveal her at the window. The window thus symbolizes absence, mourning, and a hopeless waiting for the dead; it ties him to a lost past that cannot return.

**In the prison cell**, the tiny window takes on the opposite meaning: it becomes his sole link to liberty. Through its small opening he sees a sliver of sky, a bamboo grove, and a Shiva temple. He refuses the soft bed because sitting on the cot blocks his view; watching birds fly through the window, he believes his own cage will one day break and he will "swim in that endless sky." Away from the window he sees only darkness and forgets he will ever be freed, but at the window he feels "naturally free," beyond the power of any king or emperor to hold captive—so much so that he declares the comfortable bed, not the cell, to be his true prison.

In short, the window changes from an emblem of irrevocable loss and futile hope in the bedchamber to an emblem of endurance, inner freedom, and faith in eventual liberation in the prison cell.

Initially, the relationship is a playful, transactional flirtation: the penniless but stylish guard Sitaram repeatedly visits the moneylending widow Rukmini (Mangala) to borrow cash, charming her with rhymes, mock devotion ("You are my Subhadra, and I am your Jagannath"), and self-mocking wit, while she feigns affection, teases him into reciting endearments like "Pranpriye," and lends him money she knows she will never see again—trapping him when she pointedly asks about interest and feigning hurt at his "love." Their bond deepens into secret conferring and scheming together, but it sours when Udayaditya is imprisoned: Sitaram storms to her hut, curses her, all but strikes her, and vows to burn her house, grind her face on the stone floor, and drive her from the city smeared with lime and soot. Her response is silent, gathering fury—clenched teeth, trembling fists—as she declares the Yubaraj is *hers* and that only she can do him good or harm. The final rupture comes after the staged prison fire and escape: believing Mangala dead, Sitaram sneaks into her cottage at night to loot her money, only to find her alive, drenched and spectral-looking, having returned "from the door of Yama." When he desperately revives his old feigned affection—"Are you sulking, my dear? Shall I sing that song?"—her rage only intensifies; now reckless and vengeful because the Yubaraj has shattered her hopes, she searches for a curved blade to kill him, forcing him to flee just as she hacks the floor where he stood. Realizing she knows everything about the escape and could expose him—and regretting not having strangled her—Sitaram flees Jessore with his family that same night, while Rukmini goes to Pratapaditya's court to denounce him as the arsonist and conspirator.

Sitaram's plan unfolds in escalating stages. First, he uses the fire purely as a diversion: with the help of commoners loyal to Udayaditya and palace servants, he has five or six rooms of the guards' huts set ablaze simultaneously in the evening, drawing every guard away—including the two posted at Udayaditya's door—so the prince can be led out unnoticed. Second, he prolongs the chaos: his own men join the firefighting but sabotage it by pouring water on places with no fire, failing to return with water, breaking pots, and stumbling into one another, ensuring the blaze keeps everyone occupied. Third, while attention is fixed on the guardhouse, his men quietly set fire to Udayaditya's now-empty prison cell—windows, doors, beams, rafters, doorframes, and fences—knowing no one suspects the prison could catch fire. Fourth, he transforms the blaze into evidence of death: he throws bones, a skull, and Udayaditya's sword into the burning room, then spreads shouts that the Yubaraj is screaming inside and that the roof has collapsed with no response from him. Finally, the cover-up succeeds publicly: witnesses testify at Pratapaditya's court that they saw the Yubaraj through the window during the fire, heard his screams, and produce the melted remains of his sword, so the rumor spreads that the Yubaraj perished in the flames—allowing Sitaram, as he himself reflects, to remain untroubled for some time. He further protects the deception by retrieving the letters he had sent, destroying all but those for the Mahishi and Vibha, though the scheme is ultimately threatened when Rukmini, who knows everything, survives and denounces him.

Ramchandra Ray feels no gratitude toward Udayaditya. He dismisses the rescue as something bound to happen—believing that if he were ever in peril, everyone would naturally unite to save him—and he assumes Udayaditya acted mainly for the sake of his own sister Vibha, so saving his life was not Udayaditya's true objective. Consequently, in court he joins freely in the mockery of Udayaditya, ridiculing him solely for being Pratapaditya's son, since he lacks the mental strength to silence the courtiers' taunts or refrain from joining them himself.

Pratapaditya repeatedly scoffs at the minister's warnings about the Emperor of Delhi, declaring that "the Emperor of Delhi is not my God" and even boasting that he himself will punish the Emperor. Yet this same imperial authority, which he refuses to fear, becomes the weapon turned against his own house: Bhagavat and Sitaram forge a petition—stamped with the Yubaraj Udayaditya's own seal—making it appear that the prince has lodged a complaint of treason against Pratapaditya with the Emperor in order to seize the kingdom for himself. Bhagavat then carries this forged document not to Delhi but directly to Pratapaditya, claiming he intercepted a fleeing servant of Udayaditya who was taking it toward the Emperor. Confronted with what looks like proof that his son has appealed to the very imperial power he disdains in order to betray him, Pratapaditya is enraged and turns against Udayaditya, who is thereby imprisoned. Thus the threat of Delhi that Pratapaditya once dismissed as empty anger becomes, through forgery and deception, the very mechanism of his son's downfall.

In the Jessore palace, the styling of Vibha's hair marks the intimacy between her and Surma: on the day her husband arrived, when the Mahishi imposed a hairstyle Vibha found unbearable, Vibha secretly went to Surma and had her hair done to her own liking—showing that Surma was the one who understood and tended to her wishes. After Surma's death, this same act becomes a marker of her absence: Vibha sits quietly when it is time to braid her hair, waiting as if Surma will come at any moment to braid it, but evening falls and night approaches, and Surma does not come—so Vibha's hair remains unbraided. The unbraided hair thus becomes a silent emblem of the void left by Surma, just as her unkempt hair later draws Rammohan's notice of her neglect and sorrow.
